deep.reconstruction:
This page continues Riemann's student essay 'Versuch einer allgemeinen Auffassung der Integration und Differentiation' (dated 1847, printed posthumously in the Gesammelte Werke, 1876). The previous page defines a generalized 'Ableitung' (derivative of order nu) through a two-sided expansion
  z(x+h) = sum_{nu in nu0+Z} k_nu * (d^nu z/dx^nu) * h^nu,   (2)
in which the exponents differ by integers. The factor k_nu, depending only on nu, is to be chosen so that (2) reduces to Taylor's series when the exponents are integers. That requires k_n = 1/n! for integer n. In the essay it later becomes 1/Gamma(nu+1); this is my addition from the continuation, not something on this page.

This page contains no formulas or derivations. It is a methodological interlude.
(a) Before fixing k_nu, Riemann says he will first make some remarks on series of form (2), because they are the foundation of the whole attempt at a theory of Ableitungen.
(b) He reports the view that sound conclusions can be drawn from series only when the quantities in them take values that make the series converge. Here convergence means that an (at least approximate) value can be found by a finite addition of figures.
(c) He rejects this view. When the coefficients obey a definite law, as is always assumed here, every individual part of the series can be stated exactly. The series is therefore an exactly delimited and hence determinate quantity. That the 'mechanism of addition of figures' cannot produce its value is, for him, no reason to refuse to apply the laws proved for numerical quantities, or to refuse to accept the results so obtained as correct. This is a formalist, Euler-style defence of manipulating divergent series governed by a coefficient law.
(d) He announces an example showing that a series of form (2) can really be given a value. The example uses a procedure applicable in many cases. As the next page shows, it is the expansion of x^mu in fractional powers of (x-b).

The continuation on the next page, restated so it can be checked:
- Set z = sum_alpha c_alpha (x-b)^alpha, with alpha in alpha0+Z.
- The equation mu*z - x*z' = 0 gives, after writing x = (x-b)+b and comparing coefficients, the recurrence (mu-alpha)*c_alpha = b*(alpha+1)*c_{alpha+1}.
- This is solved by c_alpha = C * b^(mu-alpha) / (Gamma(alpha+1)*Gamma(mu-alpha+1)), a generalized binomial coefficient. This closed form is my supplement.
- For integer alpha0 and C = Gamma(mu+1), this is the ordinary binomial series of x^mu = (b+(x-b))^mu.
errors: No mathematical errors are possible on this page, since it contains no computations.

The argument in (c) is philosophically contestable by modern standards. Whether a divergent series has a definite value depends on the summation method, so 'determinate quantity' is unjustified as stated. Riemann's own later rigorous practice (for example the trigonometric-series Habilitation) is far more careful. Two-sided series in alpha0+Z of the kind used next are a classic case where different summation conventions give different values; compare Hardy's analysis of 'Riemann's form of Taylor's series'.
The next-page recurrence (mu-alpha)c_alpha - b(alpha+1)c_{alpha+1} = 0 is correctly derived from mu*z - x*z' = 0.

results.what: Methodological defence of applying ordinary algebraic laws to divergent series whose coefficients follow a definite law, treating them as determinate quantities.
results.modern_name: Formal/divergent series philosophy (pre-Cauchy formalism, Euler tradition); later replaced by summability theory
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (18th c.); opposed by Cauchy and Abel (1820s)

results.what: Plan of a generalized (fractional-order) derivative defined via a two-sided series z(x+h) = sum k_nu D^nu z h^nu with exponents in nu0+Z.
results.modern_name: Riemann's fractional Taylor series; Riemann-Liouville fractional calculus
results.usually_credited_to: Liouville (1832) and Riemann (1847, publ. 1876); series studied by Hardy (1945)

results.what: Announced example: expansion of x^mu in fractional powers of (x-b).
results.modern_name: Generalized binomial series sum_{alpha in alpha0+Z} binom(mu,alpha) b^(mu-alpha) (x-b)^alpha

deep.surprise_reason: This page belongs to Riemann's 1847 student essay on generalized integration and differentiation, which has been published in his Werke since 1876 and is well known as the origin of the 'Riemann' in Riemann-Liouville. The page holds only a philosophical remark on divergent series and an announcement of an example.

checkable.sympy: a,mu,b,t=symbols('a mu b t'); c=lambda k: b**(mu-k)/(gamma(k+1)*gamma(mu-k+1)); simplify(gammasimp((mu-a)*c(a)-b*(a+1)*c(a+1)))
checkable.asserts: c_alpha = b^(mu-alpha)/(Gamma(alpha+1)Gamma(mu-alpha+1)) satisfies the next-page recurrence (mu-alpha)c_alpha = b(alpha+1)c_{alpha+1}; the result should be 0.

checkable.sympy: x,b,mu,a=symbols('x b mu a'); u=x-b; expand(mu*u**a - x*diff(u**a,x) - ((mu-a)*u**a - b*a*u**(a-1)))
checkable.asserts: Termwise, mu*(x-b)^a - x*d/dx (x-b)^a = (mu-a)(x-b)^a - b*a*(x-b)^(a-1); shifting the index gives the coefficient formula on the next page. The result should be 0.
k_nu = 1/Gamma(nu+1) reduces to the Taylor factor 1/n! for integer nu, which is the compatibility requirement stated before this page.

transcription_corrections: 'Maschinismus[?]' is most likely 'Mechanismus' ('der Mechanismus der Zifferaddition'), as in the Werke text.
'Zifferaddition' may be 'Ziffernaddition' in the hand; the meaning is the same.

In 'keinen Grund, warum wir nicht die Gesetze ...', the struck word before 'warum' and the struck 'nicht' before 'auf sie anwenden' are correctly marked as deletions, with 'nicht' inserted above the line after 'wir'.
